summary: Introduces the STD subseries of notes within the RFC series. STDs identify clearly which RFCs document Internet standards, so people can tell standards from other documents.

plainLanguage.summary: Many documents in the RFC series are just notes; only some are official Internet standards. This memo introduces the STD label that marks the official ones. The label belongs to the standard itself, so it stays the same when a newer document replaces the old one.

subtitle: How the STD subseries labels which RFCs document Internet standards, and how STD numbers work.

tldr.problem: Readers could not easily tell which RFCs documented Internet standards and which were other kinds of notes.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB creates the STD subseries. A specification that reaches the Standard maturity level gets an STD number, and the standard keeps that number even when a new document replaces it.
tldr.outcome: An STD number identifies a standard while an RFC number identifies a document. The memo is Informational and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 1311 is an Informational memo and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. Its list of STD numbers is the grandfathered set as of March 1992.

sections.title: What the STD Subseries Is
sections.content: The STDs are a subseries of notes within the RFC series that are the Internet standards. The intent is to identify clearly for the Internet community which RFCs document Internet standards. They stay inside the RFC series because its distribution and maintenance mechanisms are already in place, so anyone who can get an RFC can get an STD, and anyone who knows the RFC series can find the STDs.
sections.plainLanguage: STD is a label on the RFCs that are official rules. It lets a reader pick out the standards quickly from all the other notes.

sections.title: How STD Numbers Work
sections.content:
An STD number is assigned when a specification reaches the Standard maturity level and the IAB has designated it a standard for the Internet. Both Technical Specifications and Applicability Statements qualify. The standard for a particular protocol always keeps the same STD number.

An STD number identifies a standard, not a document. If the specification of one standard is spread over several documents, they each carry the same number. The Domain Name System is specified by RFC 1034 and RFC 1035, both labelled STD-13, so the full citation is "STD-13/RFC-1034/RFC-1035". If a standard is reworked into a new document, the new document has a new RFC number but the same STD number, and no version numbers are attached to STD numbers.

Separate STD numbers are used when the specifications are logically separable, as with the Telnet Options. Amendments and non-optional extensions reuse the base number. The memo summarizes the idea this way: an acronym such as TCP refers to a concept, a protocol; an RFC number such as RFC 793 indicates a specific version of the specification; and an STD number such as STD-7 designates the status of the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: One number names a standard, and it does not change when the standard is rewritten. A document has its own RFC number, but the standard it belongs to keeps its STD number.

sections.title: Format Rules and Publication
sections.content:
Because STDs are part of the RFC series, they follow the format rules of RFC 1111. Each STD RFC must have a "Status of this Memo" section on its first page that conveys the status approved by the IAB, a distribution statement (normally "Distribution of this memo is unlimited."), a Security Considerations section, and an author's address at the very end giving name, postal address, telephone number and email address.

New documents can become STD RFCs only through an action of the IAB, and the RFC Editor publishes them. They are announced to the RFC distribution list and obtained the same way as any RFC. The current standards are listed in the "IAB Official Protocol Standards", which is STD-1, with RFC 1280 as its current edition at the time.
sections.plainLanguage: Each official document must follow the same checklist: a note on its status, a note that anyone may share it, a section on security, and the author's address. Only the IAB can turn a document into an STD.

sections.title: The Grandfathered STDs
sections.content: The appendix assigns STD numbers to the standards that already existed. Examples include STD 5 for IP, ICMP and IGMP, STD 6 for UDP, STD 7 for TCP, STD 9 for FTP and STD 13 for the Domain Name System. STDs 27 to 32 cover Telnet options. Several entries combine more than one RFC under a single STD, such as STDs 5, 13 and 20.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendix is the first list for the new label. The standards that already existed were given their numbers all at once.
